## Introduction

A seizure involves a surge of abnormal electrical activity within the brain and may cause uncontrollable movements, temporary loss of consciousness, or other neurologic manifestations. Epilepsy refers to a condition characterized by recurrent unprovoked seizures. An epileptic seizure represents a transient occurrence of signs or symptoms resulting from abnormal, excessive, and synchronous neuronal activity in the brain. Seizures encompass multiple clinical types, with the current classification recognizing 2 major categories: focal and generalized.

During a focal seizure, activation initially occurs within a specific cortical region and may produce relatively simple manifestations, such as motor or sensory phenomena. Focal seizures may rapidly undergo secondary generalization, progressing to focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures and spreading to involve all cortical areas. Generalized seizures result from diffuse cortical activation at onset. Focal-onset seizures with rapid secondary generalization represent the most common seizure type in adults. Additional generalized seizure types include absence, atonic (drop), clonic, tonic, myoclonic, and tonic-clonic.

Epileptic syndromes provide a framework for condensing clinical information into useful nomenclature. Localization-related epilepsy denotes seizures arising from pathology within a localizable area of the brain. Idiopathic epilepsy involves no symptoms other than seizures, whereas symptomatic epilepsy reflects an underlying identifiable brain disease. Cryptogenic epilepsy describes seizure disorders suspected to result from underlying brain disease without definitive evidence confirming the specific cause. Determining whether an initial seizure or recurrent seizures are provoked or unprovoked remains fundamentally important for accurate diagnosis and appropriate treatment.

Generalized convulsive status epilepticus refers to a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting longer than 5 minutes or to multiple seizures occurring without a return to normal consciousness between episodes. Focal status epilepticus involves a focal seizure lasting longer than 10 minutes with impaired awareness. Prolonged or recurrent seizure activity during status epilepticus can result in neuronal injury, disability, coma, and death when left untreated. Rapid evaluation and prompt pharmacologic treatment of prolonged seizures therefore remain paramount.

Other paroxysmal spells may arise from central nervous system disorders, cardiac disturbances, psychiatric causes, or other etiologies. The differential diagnosis of a transient event accompanied by abnormal movements includes syncope, convulsive concussion, convulsive syncope, rigors, movement disorders, sleep-related events, and psychogenic nonepileptic seizures.

## Etiology

Seizures may be either provoked or unprovoked. Provoked seizures, also known as acute symptomatic seizures, may result from electrolyte disorders, toxins, head injury, infectious processes, vascular anomalies, tumors or other mass lesions, and many other causes. A listing of provoked causes of seizures is lengthy and could include complications of almost any disease process. Some common causes include:

Electrolyte disturbances (eg, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hypernatremia, hypocalcemia)

Acute toxic effects (eg, antidepressants, sympathomimetics)

Withdrawal syndromes (eg, ethanol, benzodiazepines)

Irregularity with prescribed antiepileptic medications

Sepsis

CNS infections

Hypoxic brain injury

Traumatic brain injury

Stroke (ischemic or hemorrhagic)

Neoplasm

Inflammatory (eg, lupus cerebritis, anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis)

Fever

Sleep deprivation

Epilepsy occurs because of a predisposition to seizures from genetic susceptibility or a chronic pathological process. By definition, unprovoked seizures occur in the absence of provocative causes or more than 7 days after an acute injury or insult, eg, stroke or brain hemorrhage. Recurrent unprovoked seizures define epilepsy. Of patients in United States general hospitals presenting with generalized convulsive status epilepticus, roughly 25% are patients with epilepsy with breakthrough seizures, medication irregularity, or new-onset epilepsy; 25% are patients with ethanol-related seizures, and 50% are patients with seizures that are provoked by a variety of medical conditions.

## Pathophysiology

Everyone has some propensity to have seizures. The concept of a seizure threshold means that each individual exists on a seizure-susceptibility continuum, with multiple factors influencing susceptibility. Medications, genetic factors, electrolyte abnormalities, sleep state, infections, brain inflammation, or injury from many causes may lead to an individual crossing that threshold with a resulting seizure.

At the cellular level, seizures begin with the excitation of susceptible cerebral neurons, which leads to synchronous discharges of progressively larger groups of interconnected neurons. Neurotransmitters are undoubtedly involved. Glutamate is the most common excitatory neurotransmitter, and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) is an important inhibitory neurotransmitter. An imbalance between excessive excitation and reduced inhibition initiates abnormal electrical activity. These electrical paroxysmal depolarization shifts (PDS) seem to trigger epileptiform activity. Increased activation or decreased inhibition of such discharges could result in seizures. The brain region affected often manifests as clinical signs or symptoms of the seizure.

Generalized convulsive status epilepticus produces systemic physiologic changes, including lactic acidosis, increased catecholamine levels, hyperthermia, respiratory compromise, and other systemic alterations. Ongoing excessive electrical activity during status epilepticus can cause brain injury. Generalized convulsive status epilepticus may evolve from continuous or discrete seizures into a state characterized by minimal or absent motor activity. Electroencephalographic activity also evolves during this progression. This evolution can culminate in nonconvulsive generalized status epilepticus, underscoring the importance of continued clinical assessment and EEG monitoring when motor manifestations diminish or cease.

## History and Physical

Clinical history plays a central role in seizure assessment and guides subsequent evaluation. The clinician should first determine from the caregiver whether the event represented a seizure or another type of transient episode. A convulsive seizure commonly presents with sudden alteration in consciousness accompanied by motor activity. Generalized seizures with motor manifestations typically begin with a stiffening or tonic phase followed by rhythmic clonic movements. A noise or cry may occur at seizure onset. Some patients report a prodrome or aura before the event. Urinary incontinence may occur but does not consistently accompany seizures. When tongue biting occurs, the injury most often involves the lateral aspect of the tongue. Following a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, patients commonly experience a transient alteration in consciousness known as the postictal state.

Seizures encompass many presentations beyond generalized convulsions. Any transient alteration in consciousness, unusual behavior, or individualized perceptual experience may represent a seizure. Key historical assessment should address prior seizure history, medication use, past medical history, and social history, with particular attention to alcohol or illicit drug use. A history of immunosuppression or malignancy also requires careful consideration. Patients may have experienced previous episodes of unresponsiveness that, in retrospect, could represent seizures. Information about events immediately preceding the episode remains particularly valuable, and friends, family members, or coworkers may provide crucial observations that the patient cannot recall.

For patients with known epilepsy, clinicians should specifically ask about irregularities in medication use. The physical examination should include both general and neurologic assessments, with particular attention to focal neurologic deficits. Witnesses may describe open eyes, lack of response to verbal or painful stimulation, and rhythmic, synchronous motor movements during a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. When a patient with suspected seizure activity has persistent altered consciousness, clinicians should consider transformed status epilepticus. Also termed subtle status epilepticus, this form of nonconvulsive status epilepticus may produce only nystagmic eye movements, facial twitching, or extremity twitching, while some patients demonstrate no motor activity at all.
